questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Value of a Function of a Jordan Block
questions.problem:
Let ${J}_{n}(\lambda )$ denote an $n\times n$ Jordan block with $\lambda $ on the main diagonal. Fill in the missing entries in the matrix below.

| ${({J}_{2}(5))}^{3}=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} |  |  |
questions.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=[\begin{aligned}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{aligned}].
$$

In this case, we have $f(x)={x}^{3},$ $n=2,$ and $\lambda =5.$
Since $n=2,$ we need to compute the first $2-1=1$ derivatives of $f:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{3} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =3{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{2}(5)) & =[\begin{aligned}f(5) & {f}^{′}(5) \\ 0 & f(5)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{5}^{3} & 3\cdot {5}^{2} \\ 0 & {5}^{3}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}125 & 75 \\ 0 & 125\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Let ${J}_{n}(\lambda )$ denote an $n\times n$ Jordan block with $\lambda $ on the main diagonal. Fill in the missing entries in the matrix below.

|  |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} | {{field-3}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\operatorname{tan}⁡({J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{4}))=\,\,$ |  | $0$ | {{field-4}} | {{field-5}} |  |
|  |  | $0$ | $0$ | {{field-6}} |  |
questions.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=[\begin{aligned}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{aligned}].
$$

In this case, we have $f(x)=\operatorname{tan}⁡x,$ $n=3,$ and $\lambda =\frac{\pi }{4}.$

Since $n=3,$ we need to compute the first $3-1=2$ derivative of $f:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & ={sec}^{2}⁡x \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =2{sec}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{3}(\pi )) & =[\begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{4}) & {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & \frac{1}{2!}{f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ 0 & f(\frac{\pi }{4}) & {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ 0 & 0 & f(\frac{\pi }{4})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) & {sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) & \frac{1}{2}\cdot 2{sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ 0 & \operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) & {sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ 0 & 0 & \operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Value of a Function of a Jordan Decomposition
questions.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
E=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}],\,J=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $E=PJ{P}^{-1},$ find $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi E).$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and matrices $A$ and $S,$ where $S$ is invertible, we have

$$
f(SA{S}^{-1})=S\cdot f(A)\cdot {S}^{-1}.
$$

For $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)$ and the given matrix $E,$ we have

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi E)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi PJ{P}^{-1})=P\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi J)\cdot {P}^{-1}.
$$

Now, since $J$ is a Jordan block with $2$s on the main diagonal, we have

$$
f(J)=[\begin{aligned}f(2) & {f}^{′}(2) \\ 0 & f(2)\end{aligned}].
$$

The derivative of $f$ is ${f}^{′}(x)=-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x).$ So, we get

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi E)=[\begin{aligned}f(2) & {f}^{′}(2) \\ 0 & f(2)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi ) & -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi ) \\ 0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Also, the inverse of $P$ is

$$
{P}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1\cdot 3-1\cdot 2}[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}cos(\pi E) & =P\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi J))\cdot {P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Value of a Function of a Jordan Matrix
questions.problem:
Let ${J}_{n}(\lambda )$ denote an $n\times n$ Jordan block with $\lambda $ on the main diagonal. Fill in the missing entries in the matrix below.

|  |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} | {{field-3}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${e}^{({J}_{2}(2)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(1))}=\,\,$ |  | $0$ | {{field-4}} | $0$ |  |
|  |  | $0$ | $0$ | {{field-5}} |  |
questions.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=[\begin{aligned}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{aligned}].
$$

First, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{({J}_{2}(2)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(1))} & ={e}^{([\begin{aligned}{J}_{2}(2) & 0 \\ 0 & {J}_{1}(1)\end{aligned}])} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{({J}_{2}(2))} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{({J}_{1}(1))}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={e}^{({J}_{2}(2))}\,⊕\,{e}^{({J}_{1}(1))}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we compute the function of each Jordan block separately.

- For ${J}_{2}(2),$ we have $n=2$ and $\lambda =2.$ since $n=2,$ we need to compute the first derivative of $f$ only:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={e}^{x} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & ={e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{2}(2)) & =[\begin{aligned}f(2) & {f}^{′}(2) \\ 0 & f(2)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2} & {e}^{2} \\ 0 & {e}^{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- For ${J}_{1}(1),$ we have $n=1$ and $\lambda =1.$ \since $n=1,$ we don't need any derivatives. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{1}(1)) & =[\begin{aligned}f(1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{(1)}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}e\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{({J}_{2}(1)\,⊕\,{J}_{2}(2))} & ={e}^{({J}_{2}(1))}\,⊕\,{e}^{({J}_{2}(2))} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2} & {e}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & e\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Value of a Function of a Jordan Matrix
questions.problem:
Let ${J}_{n}(\lambda )$ denote an $n\times n$ Jordan block with $\lambda $ on the main diagonal. Fill in the missing entries in the matrix below.

|  |  | {{field-1}} | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${({J}_{1}(3)\,⊕\,{J}_{3}(5))}^{2}=\,\,$ |  | $0$ | {{field-2}} | {{field-3}} | $1$ |  |
|  | $0$ | $0$ | $25$ | {{field-4}} |  |  |
|  |  | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | {{field-5}} |  |
questions.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=[\begin{aligned}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{aligned}].
$$

First, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{({J}_{1}(3)\,⊕\,{J}_{3}(5))}^{2} & ={([\begin{aligned}{J}_{1}(3) & 0 \\ 0 & {J}_{3}(5)\end{aligned}])}^{2} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{({J}_{1}(3))}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & {({J}_{3}(5))}^{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={({J}_{1}(3))}^{2}\,⊕\,{({J}_{3}(5))}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we compute the function of each Jordan block separately.

- For ${J}_{1}(3),$ we have $n=1$ and $\lambda =3.$ since $n=1,$ we don't need any derivatives. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{1}(3)) & =[\begin{aligned}f(3)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{3}^{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- For ${J}_{3}(5),$ we have $n=3$ and $\lambda =2.$ \since $n=3,$ we need to compute the first and second derivatives of $f$ only:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{2} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =2x \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{3}(5)) & =[\begin{aligned}f(5) & {f}^{′}(5) & \frac{{f}^{″}(5)}{2} \\ 0 & f(5) & {f}^{′}(5) \\ 0 & 0 & f(5)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{5}^{2} & 2\cdot 5 & 1 \\ 0 & {5}^{2} & 2\cdot 5 \\ 0 & 0 & {5}^{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}25 & 10 & 1 \\ 0 & 25 & 10 \\ 0 & 0 & 25\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}({J}_{1}(3)\,⊕\,{J}_{3}(5)) & =({J}_{1}(3))\,⊕\,({J}_{3}(5)) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 25 & 10 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 25 & 10 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 25\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
